transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name] — what brings you in to see me today?

I'm just... I'm here because of the voices. I keep hearing them. It's usually when I'm alone in my apartment, or sometimes if I go to the museum and it's quiet. Just... these women whispering. Like they're behind the walls, telling me which photographs belong in the archive.
How long have you been hearing these voices - is this something that just started recently, or has it been going on for a while?
It's not recent. I suppose... maybe about eight months? That's how long the whispering has been going on. And... about as long as I've been certain that people are watching my archive, too.

During these past eight months, have you noticed periods of feeling very low, hopeless, or losing interest in things—or alternatively periods of feeling unusually elevated, energetic, or needing little sleep—alongside the voices and suspicions?

I suppose... yes. There was a time when I... I wasn't really sleeping much. Maybe just a few hours a night. I was just so focused on the archive, moving from one task to the next. But... the whispering didn't stop. Even when I was working that fast, the women were still there. And I knew... I was still sure the museum board was keeping track of what I was doing.
Have you had any recent medical illnesses, head injuries, or been using any drugs, alcohol, or new medications around the time these symptoms started?
No. I... I haven't been sick. No head injuries or anything like that. And I don't use drugs. I only take the medication my regular doctor prescribes for my blood pressure. That's all.

Aside from that time when you weren't sleeping much, have there been stretches of weeks or months when your mood and energy felt fairly normal, but you were still hearing the whispering voices or feeling that the museum board was watching you?

Yes... I suppose so. There were a few weeks, maybe a month, where I... I wasn't rushing around so much. My energy was just... normal, I guess. But the whispering didn't stop. They were still there in the apartment. And... I still knew the arts people were keeping track of my phone calls. It doesn't really go away.
Of those full eight months, roughly how many weeks would you say you were in that high-energy, barely-sleeping state, compared to the weeks where your mood and energy felt normal?

I... I don't know exactly. It's hard to keep track. But... most of it, I think. Maybe six months out of the eight. I just... I couldn't stop. Making plans, buying things for the archive, hardly sleeping at all. It was just... a lot of furious energy. For most of that time.

latest_inference.note: The patient reports psychotic symptoms (hallucinations, delusions) persisting for the full 8 months, with a manic episode (decreased need for sleep, increased energy, goal-directed activity) present for the majority (6/8 months) of that time, and a distinct ~2-month period where mood/energy was normal but psychotic symptoms continued unabated. This pattern—concurrent mood and psychotic symptoms for the majority of the illness course plus a documented period of psychosis without mood symptoms—fits diagnostic criteria for schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type, and argues against schizophrenia alone (F20.9) since mood symptoms were prominent for more than half the illness duration, not just a minor component.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports 8 months of persistent auditory hallucinations (whispering women) and persecutory delusions (being monitored/watched by the museum board). For the majority of this period (~6 months) these psychotic symptoms co-occurred with a manic syndrome: markedly decreased need for sleep, increased goal-directed activity, and heightened energy. Critically, there was also a distinct ~1-month period where mood/energy symptoms fully resolved to baseline, yet the hallucinations and delusions persisted unabated. This pattern—concurrent mood episode and psychosis for the majority of the illness course, plus psychotic symptoms present for a significant period (≥2 weeks) in the absence of a mood episode—satisfies criteria for Schizoaffective Disorder, Bipolar Type, rather than a primary mood disorder with psychotic features (which would not include psychosis outside mood episodes) or schizophrenia (which would not account for the prominent, temporally-linked manic symptoms). Medical/substance causes were ruled out (no illicit drug use, no head injury, only antihypertensive medication).
